SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) -- Walt Peters knows what it's like to fear for his life. He knows how it feels to board a plane, deploying for combat. He knows the feeling of making it home alive. Walt Peters is often among the last people soldiers see as they deploy and the first they see upon their return. That's why the retired Vietnam veteran has stood outside at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, for the past four years as a beacon of pride and support, welcoming home returning soldiers and wishing "Godspeed" to those deploying. "To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," says Peters. "These guys are our freedom." Peters, 64, has been one of the last people that about 20,000 soldiers so far have seen before boarding the plane for the war zone -- and one of the first seen upon return. No matter what time the soldiers' flights are arriving or departing -- many take place in the middle of the night -- Peters is there to shake their hands and give them a token of support: a small American flag. Some of those flags, Peters says, have gone to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'" Peters is not the only volunteer showing his support at each flight. But he does all of this nearly blind. He says learned he had chemical diabetes nearly 10 years ago after he was exposed to Agent Orange during his Vietnam tours. He has lost almost all of his sight over the past few years, but that hasn't depleted his dedication to the soldiers. "When I went to Vietnam on my tours I'd never had this. I had never had nobody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters says. "When they get on that plane, they're gonna know that this old Vietnam vet cares." Peters first became involved greeting flights through the Savannah Red Cross in 2004 when a friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge brought him to welcome a returning flight. Peters has since become a flight greeting leader, bringing in and training his own volunteers. His crew includes Moose members and Vietnam veterans. So many flights come in, Peters says, that it's impossible to be present for all of them. He's worked as many as three flights in one day, in a 26-hour period.   Watch how Peters sends off and greets deploying and returning U.S. soldiers » . Peters and his volunteers arrive two hours before a flight's arrival or departure to set up their tables and brew coffee. He makes sure he walks around and talks with the troops when they come through for processing. "I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters says. "I tell them, 'It's OK to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'" Peters also talks to the soldiers about the Adopt-A-Soldier program, asking them to fill out a card so a family can "adopt" them and send care packages and necessities to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.  Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq » . Peters says the most important thing is to show the soldiers "the support and the spirit that they need behind them as they step up to get on that plane." "Sometimes it breaks your heart because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'" But as long as there are soldiers deploying and returning, Peters says he'll be there.  Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career » . "I see the roots of our country and our future in every one of these soldiers," he says.

**SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN)** — Walt Peters understands the visceral fear of combat. He knows the heavy feeling of boarding a plane bound for war, just as he knows the profound relief of returning home alive. 

As a retired Vietnam veteran, Peters is often among the very last faces soldiers see as they deploy and the first to greet them upon their return. For the past four years, he has stood vigil at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia—a steadfast beacon of pride and support, offering a warm welcome home to returning troops and wishing "Godspeed" to those heading into harm's way. 

"To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," Peters says. "These guys are our freedom."

Now 64, Peters has served as a final, reassuring presence for roughly 20,000 soldiers embarking for war zones, and one of the first to embrace them upon their homecoming. Regardless of the hour—with many flights arriving or departing in the dead of night—Peters is invariably there. He shakes every soldier's hand and presents them with a small token of gratitude: a modest American flag. 

Some of those flags, Peters notes, have traveled to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'"

While Peters is not the only volunteer extending support at these flights, his dedication is rendered all the more extraordinary by his physical hardship: he carries out his mission nearly blind. Almost a decade ago, Peters was diagnosed with chemical diabetes stemming from his exposure to Agent Orange during his tours in Vietnam. Though he has lost nearly all of his sight in recent years, his resolve remains entirely undiminished. 

"When I went to Vietnam on my tours I'd never had this. I had never had nobody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters recalls. "When they get on that plane, they're gonna know that this old Vietnam vet cares."

Peters’ journey as a flight greeter began in 2004 through the Savannah Red Cross, after a fellow member of his fraternal Moose Lodge invited him to welcome a returning flight. Since then, Peters has stepped into the role of flight greeting leader, organizing and training his own team of volunteers, which includes fellow Moose Lodge members and Vietnam veterans. 

The sheer volume of troop movements makes it impossible to meet every single flight, Peters explains. Yet, his commitment is unwavering—he has worked up to three flights within a single 26-hour span.

*[Watch how Peters sends off and greets deploying and returning U.S. soldiers]*

For every mission, Peters and his volunteers arrive two hours prior to a flight's scheduled arrival or departure to set up information tables and brew coffee. He makes a point of walking among the troops, offering a comforting word as they move through processing. 

"I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters says. "I tell them, 'It's OK to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'"

Peters also introduces the troops to the Adopt-A-Soldier program, encouraging them to complete contact cards so American families can "adopt" them, sending care packages and essential supplies during their deployments in Iraq or Afghanistan.

*[Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq]*

Ultimately, Peters believes the most crucial part of his work is instilling the troops with "the support and the spirit that they need behind them as they step up to get on that plane."

It is an emotional endeavor that carries a heavy weight. "Sometimes it breaks your heart because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'"

Yet, as long as service members continue to deploy and return, Peters vows he will be there to meet them.

*[Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career]*

"I see the roots of our country and our future in every one of these soldiers," he says.

Day or night, regardless of the hour, retired Vietnam veteran Walt Peters can be found at Hunter Army Airfield in Georgia. His mission is simple yet profoundly moving: to ensure that every soldier deploying to or returning from military service receives a proper hero’s welcome. 

Peters’ journey as a troop greeter began in 2004 through a partnership with a local fraternal lodge and the Savannah Red Cross. By standing at the gates of Hunter Army Airfield, he provides today’s troops with the gratitude, respect, and unwavering support that he and his fellow veterans were so unfairly denied.

counterfactuals.output:
**SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN)** — The humidity of a coastal Georgia midnight hangs thick over the tarmac at Hunter Army Airfield. The roar of a commercial charter jet cuts through the dark as its engines slowly whine down to a hum.

On the asphalt below, dressed in a worn leather jacket and a black ballcap embroidered with the words *Vietnam Veteran*, 76-year-old Walt Peters adjusts his stance. His joints ache in the damp night air, but he doesn’t sit down. He hasn't sat down for a flight arrival in over twelve years.

As the plane’s door opens, a wave of young men and women in operational camouflage fatigues begins file down the air stairs. They are exhausted, carrying heavy sea bags, their faces etched with the lingering tension of a nine-month deployment to the Middle East.

Then they hit the bottom step, and they hit Walt. 

"Welcome home, brother," Peters says, his voice a low, raspy rumble as he pulls a 20-year-old sergeant into a sudden, firm bear hug. "We’re proud of you. Job well done."

The sergeant looks startled for a second, then his shoulders drop. The tension drains from his face. "Thank you, sir," the young soldier whispers back.

Peters lets go, steps aside, and reaches for the next hand. Over the next hour, he will greet all 240 soldiers on board. He will do the exact same thing when the next unit deploys at 4:00 a.m.

***

### A Debt Owed, A Vow Kept

To the commanders and soldiers of the 3rd Infantry Division stationed in Savannah, Peters is simply known as "The Sentinel of Hunter." To the USO volunteers, he’s a fixture. But to Peters himself, he is just a man trying to fix a decades-old wrong.

In 1969, Peters was a 21-year-old Army Corporal landing at Travis Air Force Base in California after a grueling 13-month tour in the Mekong Delta. He remembers the cold quiet of the terminal. He remembers being told to change into civilian clothes as fast as possible to avoid protesters outside the gates. 

"Nobody said 'thank you.' Nobody said 'good job,'" Peters recalls, his blue eyes watery as he looks out over the runway. "You just took your uniform off, packed your bad memories away, and tried to pretend you were never there. It left a hole in a lot of us. A dark hole."

Decades passed. Peters built a life, worked as a mechanic, raised a family, and eventually retired to Savannah. But the memory of that quiet, lonely return home never fully faded.

In 2012, after hearing that a local brigade was returning from Afghanistan in the dead of night, Peters drove to the airfield. He stood behind the barricades and started clapping. 

He hasn't stopped coming back since.

"I made a promise to myself," Peters says, his hand resting on the silver Vietnam Service ribbon pinned to his chest. "As long as there is breath in my lungs, no young man or woman wearing this uniform will ever leave this country, or come back to it, without knowing they are loved. Period."

***

### 'He fills a gap'

At Hunter Army Airfield, one of the U.S. military’s primary departure points for rapid-deployment forces, flights come and go at all hours. Schedules shift constantly due to weather, maintenance, and tactical delays. 

Yet, rain or shine, 3:00 p.m. or 3:00 a.m., Peters is there. The USO contacts him whenever a bird is coming in or rolling out. 

For the young service members, many of whom are leaving American soil for the first time—or returning to empty terminals while their families wait for them back in distant hometowns—Peters’ presence is a powerful anchor.

"When you get off that plane, you're numb," says Spc. Marcus Vance, 22, who just returned from a rotation in Eastern Europe. "You've been traveling for 24 hours. You're exhausted, you miss your family. And then this guy grabs your hand, looks you dead in the eye, and says he’s proud of you. You can tell he means it. It hits you right in the chest."

Commanders on the base say Peters’ quiet mission provides something the military, for all its logistics and structure, cannot manufacture.

"Walt fills a gap that only someone who has walked in those boots can fill," says Lt. Col. Sarah Jenkins. "He bridges the generation gap. He shows these young soldiers that their service matters, not just to the military, but to the nation. He is the heart of this airfield."

***

### Healing on the Tarmac

Psychologists who study combat veterans often talk about the concept of "moral injury" and the long path to healing trauma. For Peters, the tarmac at Hunter has become a sanctuary—a place where the ghosts of 1969 are slowly laid to rest.

"People tell me I'm doing a great thing for these kids," Peters says, watching the bus full of soldiers roll away toward the barracks, their shadows long under the stadium lights. "But they don't understand. These kids are doing it for me."

He pauses, watching the red taillights of the bus disappear into the night. 

"Every time I hug one of them, every time I say 'welcome home,' a little piece of that old bitterness goes away," he says, a soft smile breaking through his weathered face. "I'm finally coming home, too."

As the airfield quieted down around 2:30 a.m., Peters walked back to his pickup truck. He had a couple of hours to sleep before the next transport plane was scheduled to take off for Europe. 

He’ll be back on the tarmac before the engines start.

counterfactuals.output:
The hum of the jet engines doesn’t reach Arthur “Artie” Vance through his eyes, but through the soles of his boots. Sitting in a worn vinyl chair in Gate 4B of the regional airfield, the 76-year-old Marine Corps veteran feels the low-frequency rumble in his chest long before the flashing lights of the charter flight register as pale, milky blurs in his peripheral vision.

To the casual observer, Artie might look like a man out of place. He wears a crisp dress shirt, a neatly pinned Marine Corps cap, and dark sunglasses that cover eyes clouded by severe glaucoma and an old shrapnel injury from his time in Danang. Resting against his knee is a folding white cane. 

To the airport staff, however, Artie is as permanent a fixture as the flight boards. Three nights a week—often at two or three in the morning—he sits right here, waiting.

"They’re off the plane, Artie," whispers Sarah, a night-shift gate agent, placing a gentle hand on his shoulder. "About a hundred and fifty of 'em. Coming down the jetway now."

Artie nods, his posture instantly shifting. The slump of an elderly man vanishes, replaced by the rigid, proud alignment of a Sergeant who served in 1968. He stands up, adjusts his cap, and plant his feet.

For Artie, the world has been dark for nearly fifteen years, reduced to vague shadows and high-contrast light. But as the heavy double doors swing open and the sound of military boots strikes the linoleum floor, his senses ignite. He doesn't need sight to map the room. He hears the rhythmic, heavy clatter of duffel bag buckles, the rustle of stiff camouflage fabric, the quiet, exhausted murmurs of young men and women returning from a nine-month deployment in the Middle East.

He smells the distinct cocktail of jet fuel, stale cabin air, and sweat. 

As the first soldier steps into the terminal, Artie steps forward, extending his right hand into the void. 

"Welcome home, Sergeant," Artie says, his voice carrying the deep, gravelly warmth of a man who knows the exact weight of a combat deployment.

A young man pauses, startled. He looks at Artie’s cane, then at the bright yellow Marine Corps insignia on his cap, and finally at the outstretched, weathered hand. The young soldier grips it firmly.

"Thank you, sir," the soldier replies, his voice cracking slightly with exhaustion.

Artie covers the young man’s hand with his left. "Good to have you back on American soil, son. You did good."

For the next forty-five minutes, Artie stands in the current of returning troops. He doesn't move from his post. He shakes hands—hundreds of them. He reads the soldiers not with his eyes, but through the calluses on their palms, the tension in their forearms, and the tremor in their voices. 

When a young woman stops in front of him, Artie senses her hesitation. He hears the slight, rapid hitch in her breathing. 

"Specialist?" Artie asks softly, reaching out.

"Yes, sir," she whispers. 

Artie offers her a small, metal challenge coin he keeps in his pocket—a habit he’s maintained since he started greeting flights eight years ago. "Put this in your pocket. Whenever you feel like you're still over there, hold onto it and remember you're back here."

She breaks into a quiet sob, stepping forward to wrap her arms around the old Marine's neck. Artie pat her back gently, holding her until she steps back, wiping her eyes, and moves toward the baggage claim where her family waits.

People often ask Artie why a blind man, who lives an hour’s drive away and relies on a rotating schedule of volunteer drivers, spends his sleep-deprived nights in a drafty airport terminal. 

The answer lies in a memory from 1969.

When Artie returned from Vietnam, wounded and confused, there was no crowd at the airport. There were no handshakes, no hand-painted banners, no warm coffee. He walked through a silent, cold terminal alone, feeling like a ghost returning to a world that wished he had stayed dead.

"I decided a long time ago that as long as I have breath in my lungs, no kid stepping off a plane in a uniform is ever going to feel the way I felt that night," Artie says, his thumb tracing the brass edge of his Marine Corps belt buckle. "I can't see their faces. I don't know what color their eyes are, or if they're smiling or crying. But I know what's in their hearts, because I carried it too. You don't need eyes to see that."

By 4:00 AM, the terminal has cleared. The laughter and tearful reunions have moved to the parking lot and melted into the night. The airfield is quiet again, save for the hum of the cleaning crew's floor buffers.

Artie sits back down in his chair, folding his cane with a series of sharp clicks. He looks tired, but there is a quiet, indestructible peace in his face. 

Sarah, the gate agent, walks over with two paper cups of hot coffee, handing one to Artie. 

"That was the last flight for tonight, Artie," she says softly. "Your ride will be here in twenty minutes."

Artie takes a sip, feeling the warmth of the cup between his hands, and smiles into the dark. 

"Good," he says quietely. "That means they're all home."

**FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.** — On a crisp Tuesday morning at the military terminal, the air is thick with the nervous energy of young men and women preparing to deploy overseas. Dressed in modern camouflage, soldiers move in quiet, disciplined lines. But standing near the boarding gate is a fixture of calm and warmth: 64-year-old Walt Peters. 

Leaning heavily on a cane, his hands tremor slightly—a physical souvenir of a war fought decades ago. Yet, as each soldier passes, Peters reaches into a wooden crate beside him, hands them a small, hand-held American flag, and offers four simple words: "Thank you. Come home."

**[Watch: Walt Peters greets deploying troops at Fort Liberty terminal]**

Peters, a Vietnam War veteran, is a volunteer with the American Red Cross Service to the Armed Forces program. For the past six years, he has made it his personal mission to ensure no modern service member leaves American soil—or returns to it—without a hero's farewell.

For Peters, the duty is deeply personal. As an 18-year-old combat soldier in the early 1970s, he spent months navigating the dense, humid jungles of Southeast Asia. Decades after the fighting stopped, the war caught up with him. Peters suffers from aggressive peripheral neuropathy, heart complications, and severe respiratory issues—all medical conditions linked directly to his exposure to Agent Orange, the toxic herbicide sprayed widely during the conflict.

"My body is fighting a battle every single day," Peters says, adjusting his red volunteer vest. "Some days, the pain makes it hard to get out of bed. But the moment I pull up to this airfield and see these young kids in uniform, the pain just fades into the background."

**[Watch: "It took my health, but not my heart": Walt Peters opens up about his battle with Agent Orange]**

The quiet tragedy of Peters’ generation of veterans was the homecoming—or lack thereof. When Peters returned to the United States after his tour, there were no brass bands, no welcoming committees, and no flags. 

"We came home to silence, or worse," Peters recalls, his eyes misting over. "Nobody gave us a flag. Nobody said 'thank you.' I swore to myself that as long as I have breath in my lungs, I won't let another generation of soldiers feel forgotten."

That oath led him to the Red Cross, where he quickly became one of the region’s most beloved volunteers. Rain or shine, day or night flight, Peters is there. To date, he estimates he has placed more than 40,000 miniature stars and stripes into the hands of deploying troops, returning veterans, and military families.

For the soldiers walking past his station, the brief encounter leaves a lasting impression. 

"Meeting Mr. Peters gives you perspective," says Private First Class Marcus Vance, 20, holding the small flag Peters gave him moments earlier. "He went through hell, both over there and coming back. For him to stand out here for hours just to shake our hands... it means everything."

**[Watch: Young soldiers react to meeting Vietnam veteran Walt Peters before departure]**

Despite his declining physical health and frequent medical appointments at the local VA hospital, Peters has no plans to slow down. The wooden crate of flags sits by his front door at home, ready for the next call from the Red Cross dispatch coordinator.

"People tell me I'm doing something great for these kids," Peters says, offering a warm, tired smile as the final soldier walks onto the tarmac. "But the truth is, they're the ones saving me. Giving away these flags... it's the best medicine I’ve ever been prescribed."

counterfactuals.output:
**THE ECHO OF HONOR**

*Arthur Vance returned from war to a wall of silence. Now, at 76, he makes sure no modern soldier ever walks through an airport terminal alone.*

**By [Author Name]**

It is 2:45 a.m. inside the cavernous, dimly lit terminal of the international airport. The shops are shuttered, the concourse is hushed, and most of the city is asleep. But near Gate B22, seventy-six-year-old Arthur “Artie” Vance is wide awake, standing at attention. 

His back is straight, though his knees ache from decades of hard labor and a long-ago brush with shrapnel in the Mekong Delta. Clutched in his right hand is a small American flag; around his neck hangs a lanyard heavy with lapel pins gifted to him by young men and women in uniform over the last twenty years.

Suddenly, the heavy door of the jet bridge opens. 

Out steps a tired column of young soldiers, fresh off a 15-hour flight from a deployment in the Middle East. They carry heavy rucksacks, their eyes rimmed with exhaustion, expecting to trudge silently through an empty airport to catch their connecting flights.

Instead, they walk straight into a wall of thunderous applause.

Leading the charge is Artie. His voice, clear and booming despite his age, cuts through the quiet night: “Welcome home! God bless you! Thank you for your service!”

For the next forty-five minutes, Artie and his small army of volunteers—mostly fellow veterans and military families—shake every hand, hug every neck, hand out homemade cookies, and offer prepaid phone cards. But more than anything, Artie offers something money cannot buy: eye contact, deep respect, and the unconditional warmth of a country saying *thank you*.

To the young men and women walking off that plane, Artie is a guardian angel in a baseball cap. But to Artie, every handshake is the payment of a long-overdue debt—one that was denied to him more than half a century ago.

***

### The Cold Arrival

In November 1969, Sergeant Artie Vance landed at Travis Air Force Base after a grueling 13-month tour in Vietnam with the 9th Infantry Division. He was twenty-one years old, carried physical and invisible scars, and desperately wanted to believe his sacrifice meant something.

Instead, his welcome home was a study in isolation.

"We were told to change into civilian clothes in the airport restroom so we wouldn’t attract trouble," Artie recalls, his voice softening. "There were no banners. No handshakes. People looked right through us, or worse, looked at us with disgust. I bought a pack of cigarettes, sat in a corner of the terminal, and took a bus home in the dark. It felt like stepping out of the jungle and straight into a deep, freezing fog."

For decades, Artie lived in that fog. He built a life—worked as a master electrician, raised three children, paid his taxes—but he buried his uniform in a trunk in the attic. The pain of his country’s apathy was a silent weight he carried every day.

Then came the early 2000s, and a new generation of Americans was sent off to war in Iraq and Afghanistan. 

"I saw the news reports of these kids—nineteen, twenty years old—shipping out," Artie says. "And I thought about how terrified they must be. But more than that, I worried about what would happen when they came back. I swore right then: *Not on my watch. Not again.*"

***

### "Operation Warm Welcome"

What started in 2004 as Artie standing alone at a gate with a cardboard sign has evolved into "Operation Warm Welcome," a non-profit volunteer network with over 200 members. Rain or shine, at 2:00 p.m. or 3:00 a.m., Artie’s group receives flight manifests and ensures that no military charter or commercial flight carrying deploying or returning troops passes through their city unnoticed.

They are there for the tearful send-offs, standing as a bulwark of encouragement, telling young recruits, "We’ll be right here waiting for you when you get back." And they are there for the homecomings, turning quiet concourses into roaring parades of gratitude.

"Artie doesn't just clap," says Sarah Jenkins, whose son deployed twice to Syria. "He looks these kids in the eye. He grips their hands. You can see the tension melt off their shoulders. He gives them permission to feel proud of what they’ve done."

The impact on the modern soldiers is profound. Captain Marcus Reed, 28, remembers stepping off the plane after his first deployment, disoriented and mentally exhausted.

"You’re in a weird headspace coming back from a war zone," Reed says. "You feel disconnected from the civilian world. Walking off that plane and seeing Mr. Vance—this Vietnam vet with tears in his eyes, saluting us—it anchored me. It made me feel like I was finally back on safe ground. He gave us the hero’s welcome he deserved, but never got."

***

### Healing Across Generations

Standing at the gate as the last soldier walks toward the baggage claim, Artie finally lets out a long breath and leans against a pillar. His hands tremble slightly, but his smile is broad. 

Over the past two decades, Artie has greeted an estimated 50,000 soldiers. In doing so, a miraculous thing happened: the cold fog of 1969 began to burn away.

"People tell me I'm doing a great service for these kids," Artie says, adjusting his cap, which reads *Vietnam Veteran - Proud to Have Served*. "But the truth is, these kids saved my life. Every time I say 'welcome home' to one of them, a little piece of the 21-year-old kid I used to be finally comes home, too."

The airport terminal begins to quiet down again. Artie packs up his spare flags, checks his watch, and makes a note of the next scheduled troop transit—a flight landing tomorrow at dawn. 

He will be there. Because as long as young men and women step forward to serve, Artie Vance will be waiting in the light, making sure the dark never touches them again.

**MIDNIGHT MISSION: How One Volunteer Leader Sends Off Hunter’s Deploying Troops with Warmth and Care**

**SAVANNAH, Ga.** — At 2:30 a.m. under the harsh glare of the tarmac floodlights at Hunter Army Airfield, the air was thick with the rumble of jet engines and the quiet tension of departing soldiers. But standing near the foot of the air stairs, armed with a clip-board, a infectious smile, and a stack of handmade cards, was Sarah Jenkins. 

For Jenkins, a retired Army veteran turned community volunteer, the middle of the night is when her most important work begins. As the team lead for the airfield’s volunteer flight greeters, her mission is simple yet profound: ensure that no soldier leaves Savannah for a deployment without feeling the support of the community behind them.

"We can’t change where they are going or the challenges they are about to face," Jenkins said, watching as dozens of soldiers from the 3rd Infantry Division, weighed down by heavy rucksacks and body armor, filed off the buses and toward the departure hangar. "But we can control the atmosphere in this room before they leave. We want their last memory on American soil for the next nine months to be one of love and gratitude."

Hunter Army Airfield serves as a critical power-projection platform for the U.S. Military, frequently sending soldiers to locations across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. Deployments often happen on short notice and at odd hours, making the work of Jenkins and her volunteer crew both demanding and crucial.

Inside the departure terminal, Jenkins moved swiftly, directing a team of a dozen volunteers. Tables were lined with hot coffee, fresh donuts, snack packs, and travel-sized hygiene items—all donated by local Savannah businesses and civic groups. Near the corner, a designated "quiet area" offered chargers, magazines, and a wall of colorful drawings created by local schoolchildren expressing thanks for the soldiers' service.

As the team lead, Jenkins acts as both a logistical conductor and an emotional anchor. She liaises with military flight coordinators to track late arrivals and gate changes, while continuously checking in on her team and the deploying service members. 

For many young soldiers, particularly those facing their first overseas deployment, the atmosphere Jenkins creates offers a sense of comfort amidst the uncertainty.

"You’re running on pure adrenaline, stress, and lack of sleep," said Sgt. 1st Class Marcus Vance, who was preparing to board a charter flight to Eastern Europe. "Then you walk into the terminal and see people who have no military obligation staying up all night just to hand you a cup of coffee and shake your hand. It changes your whole mindset. It reminds you who you're down there defending."

Jenkins’ path to this role was deeply personal. Having deployed twice during her 12 years of military service, she vividly remembers the hollow feeling of walking through quiet, empty terminals in the dead of night. When she settled in Savannah four years ago, she swore she would do everything in her power to ensure current soldiers had a different experience.

Since taking over as flight greeting leader two years ago, Jenkins has overseen the send-offs—and welcomes home—of over 15,000 service members. She keeps a logbook filled with dates, unit names, and brief notes. 

"Every flight has a story," Jenkins remarked, gesturing toward the logbook. "Sometimes it's a quiet group that just needs rest. Other times, it's a young unit that needs high-fives and a bit of energy to keep their spirits up. You learn to read the room."

As the final boarding call echoed through the terminal, Jenkins took her position near the exit door. She offered a warm firm handshake, a word of encouragement, or a quick hug to every soldier passing through. 

Within thirty minutes, the terminal emptied out. The volunteers gathered their empty boxes and folded down the tables, preparing the space for the next scheduled deployment later in the week. Outside, the charter jet taxied down the runway and lifted off into the dark Georgia sky.

Jenkins watched the blinking lights of the aircraft vanish into the clouds, taking a quiet breath before gathering her coat.

"Now, we just count down the days until we get to stand on this same tarmac and welcome them back home," she said.
